demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette:
David, a 54-year-old forester, had always found solace and purpose in the towering pines and quiet trails of the Pacific Northwest. Two years ago, that world shattered. A miscalculated cut, a sudden, powerful downdraft, and a massive Douglas fir had come crashing down not where David intended, but onto an access road, pinning his colleague, Mark, beneath its immense weight. The visceral memory of Mark’s agonised screams, the sickening *thud*, and the sight of his friend’s mangled leg were etched into David’s mind with terrifying clarity. Mark survived, but with devastating, life-altering injuries.

In the aftermath, David’s world began to shrink. A sudden twinge of **physical pain in a part of his body**, perhaps a phantom ache in his own leg, would send a jolt of anxiety through him, immediately activating a heightened sense of vigilance; he’d start scanning his surroundings, feeling an indistinct **threat** even in his own home. That same **physical pain** often served as a direct portal back to the accident, pulling him into vivid **memories** of the scene, particularly the chilling sensation of his own body stiffening, a **bodily reenactment** of bracing for impact. When these **memories** surfaced, whether as a full mental replay or the visceral **bodily reenactment**, they brought with them an overwhelming **grief** for Mark’s lost future and an intense **rage on recall**, particularly directed at himself. This emotional tempest invariably reinforced his belief that **he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him**—his profession, his identity.

His once-cherished role as a forester, a job that had defined him for decades, became a source of profound anguish. Working in the forest, the necessary **physical proximity** to other crew members, or even the sight of a familiar piece of equipment, would become unbearable **triggers**, bringing up fresh **reminders of the victim**. This constant re-exposure solidified his conviction that **there was something intrinsic about him that made the event happen**, feeding into the deep-seated **negative appraisal** that **he couldn't rely on himself**. The pervasive feeling that he was **unable to relax**, constantly **watching other people closely** for signs of danger, meant his mind was always primed for the worst. This chronic state of **threat** made it easier for **memories** of the accident to intrude, often catching him off guard during moments of perceived vulnerability, further eroding his sense of safety.

The vividness of the **memories**, especially the **bodily reenactment** of his own stance as the tree fell, made him hyper-aware of his own body, turning any minor ache into a potent **trigger** for further distress. He started avoiding the forest altogether, claiming minor ailments, leading to disciplinary warnings and a growing rift with his wife, Maria, who struggled to understand his sudden withdrawal. This heightened state of **threat**, the feeling that he was perpetually in danger, especially when **strangers approached him** on the street, transformed ordinary sensations and encounters into potent **triggers**. A sudden noise that might once have been ignored now felt like a precursor to disaster, instantly activating his fear response. His persistent sense of **threat**, the feeling that **strangers** were inherently dangerous and that he needed to **watch others** constantly, cemented his conviction that **he couldn't rely on himself** to navigate the world safely, reinforcing the **negative appraisal** that he was somehow fundamentally flawed and responsible for the harm he caused.

David now lives in a tightening spiral of fear and self-reproach. He spends his days at home, isolated, constantly on edge, the weight of his perceived failures pressing down on him. Maria’s patience is wearing thin, and David feels the unspoken question in her eyes: *What happened to the man I married?* He finally sought help, exhausted by the relentless cycle, desperately hoping to escape the prison of his mind, yet deeply afraid that his own assessment is correct – that he is, in fact, **no longer capable** of living a normal life.
